tip: Bisogna + infinitive means 'one must'; the conditional Bisognerebbe softens it to 'one should' or 'you ought to'.
For -are verbs, the future and conditional stem changes the a to e: comprare becomes Comprerei, not comprarei.
Verbs ending in -giare drop the i in the future and conditional: mangiare becomes Mangerei, never mangierei.
In hypotheticals, se + past subjunctive (avesse) pairs with the conditional in the main clause (parlerebbe).
Quella drops to quell' before a feminine word starting with a vowel: quell'offerta, not quella offerta.
Senza adds di before a pronoun: senza di noi, senza di me. Before a noun it stands alone: senza zucchero.
After senza, Italian uses the infinitive, not the -ing form: senza dirci niente = without telling us anything.
Past conditional = conditional of avere or essere plus the participle. Avrei voluto = 'I would have liked', a past regret.
With piacere the person who likes is the indirect object: a loro piacerebbe = literally 'to them it would please'.
Buono shortens to buon before a masculine singular noun: un buon lavoro, just like the article un.
For 'on Saturday' use sabato with no preposition. Adding the article, il sabato, would mean 'every Saturday'.
Informazioni is normally plural in Italian, unlike English 'information': maggiori informazioni = more information.
Andare contracts its future and conditional stem to andr-: andresti = 'you would go', not andaresti.
Use a with cities and towns: a Roma = 'in/to Rome'. Countries take in instead, as in in Italia.
Bastava che ('it was enough that') triggers the subjunctive: bastava che tu mi avvisassi.
Parlare con means to talk with a person; parlare di means to talk about a topic. Here both appear.
Italian also builds the passive with venire: verrà inaugurato = 'will be inaugurated', like sarà inaugurato.
La maggior parte ('most') takes a singular verb even with a plural: la maggior parte delle persone preferirebbe.
Cui means 'whose' between two nouns; the article agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: i cui figli.
